headline: Why Jets Still Use 1980s Floppy Disks
summary: Certified avionics remain locked to 3.5-inch floppy disks due to FAA re-certification costs and timelines. Airlines sustain obsolete supply chains while modern storage alternatives face decade-long approval barriers.
source: FAA Avionics Certification & Aviation Security Audits

slides.title: Modern Jets Still Run on 1980s Floppy Disks
slides.subtitle: Critical avionics updates depend on 3.5-inch media
slides.body: Why do certified aircraft require obsolete storage? The answer lies in rigid FAA certification and supply-chain inertia.
slides.deep_dive: Avionics systems are certified with specific hardware configurations. Changing storage media requires re-certification, a multi-year, multi-million dollar process. Airlines maintain fleets of 3.5-inch drives and source disks from dwindling suppliers.
slides.key_fact: FAA certification locks avionics to 1980s-era 3.5-inch floppy disks.
slides.why_it_matters: Engineers maintaining legacy systems face security risks and supply-chain fragility.

slides.title: Certification Barriers Outpace Modern Storage
slides.body: Re-certifying avionics for USB or solid-state storage costs millions and takes years. Airlines choose to sustain floppy supply chains instead.
slides.deep_dive: The DO-178C/DO-254 certification framework treats any hardware change as a new certification event. Economic analysis shows maintaining floppy logistics is cheaper than re-certifying fleets.
slides.key_fact: Re-certification for new storage media can exceed $10M per aircraft type.
slides.why_it_matters: Technical debt in safety-critical systems is measured in decades, not sprints.

slides.title: The Certification Lock-In Process
slides.body: A step-by-step flow shows why a simple storage swap becomes a decade-long project.
slides.deep_dive: Each step involves rigorous documentation, testing, and FAA review. The process is designed for safety, not agility.
slides.key_fact: Full re-certification cycles average 5-10 years for hardware changes.
slides.why_it_matters: Engineers must plan for hardware obsolescence at project inception.

slides.title: Legacy Supply Chain vs. Modern Alternatives
slides.body: Airlines manage niche floppy suppliers while modern storage faces regulatory walls.
slides.deep_dive: The floppy ecosystem includes specialized manufacturers and custom drive refurbishment. Modern paths require new cybersecurity audits and wireless update approvals.
slides.key_fact: Physical floppy logistics remain cheaper than certification of alternatives.
slides.why_it_matters: Security teams must audit physical media supply chains as attack vectors.

slides.title: Engineering in a Frozen Hardware World
slides.body: Software engineers build update tools for floppy images. Security researchers find air-gapped systems vulnerable to physical media tampering. Startups face high barriers to enter avionics market.
slides.deep_dive: Development workflows include floppy image creation, checksum verification, and physical delivery procedures. Threat models must account for compromised disks during transit.
slides.key_fact: Avionics update toolchains often include floppy disk emulators for testing.
slides.why_it_matters: Legacy hardware constraints dictate software architecture and security posture.

slides.title: The Long Road to Modern Avionics Updates
slides.body: Certification inertia keeps 1980s media alive. Modular certification and supply-chain audits are the path forward.
slides.deep_dive: Industry groups push for "certification credits" for hardware upgrades. Until then, floppy disks remain a critical, if anachronistic, link in aviation safety.
slides.key_fact: No certified commercial jet uses USB or network updates for primary avionics loading.
slides.why_it_matters: Strategic planning must account for decades-long hardware lifecycles.
takeaways: Expect legacy media in critical systems for decades; design tooling accordingly.
Advocate for modular certification pathways to enable incremental hardware upgrades.
Physical media supply chains are a hidden attack surface; audit them rigorously.
